content: The United Nations Commission on Narcotic Drugs, the UN General Assembly, and the UN Economic and Social Council have all endorsed a comprehensive package of harm reduction services for people who inject drugs (PWID). However, access to these services remains insufficient for this population. The comprehensive harm reduction package for PWID includes the following interventions: Needle and syringe programs. Opioid substitution therapy, other evidence-based drug dependence treatments, and naloxone for opioid overdose management. HIV testing services. Antiretroviral therapy. Prevention and treatment of sexually transmitted infections. Condom distribution programs for PWID and their sexual partners. Targeted information, education, and communication for PWID and their sexual partners. Prevention, vaccination, diagnosis, and treatment for viral hepatitis. Prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of tuberculosis (TB). In 2008, the World Health Organization (WHO), the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), and UNAIDS jointly published policy guidelines for integrating TB and HIV services for people who inject drugs. These guidelines aimed to reduce the morbidity and mortality associated with TB and HIV among people who use drugs (PWUD) and their communities. Since then, WHO has issued numerous policies and guidelines recommending life-saving interventions to address TB, HIV-associated TB, HIV, and hepatitis B and C, as well as drug dependence treatment. The updated guidelines emphasize the importance of delivering integrated, comprehensive healthcare services for PWID. They also highlight the interconnected risk factors and social determinants of TB, such as HIV, poverty, homelessness, poor nutrition, drug use, smoking, and excessive alcohol consumption. PWID have a higher prevalence of latent TB infection (LTBI) and active TB disease compared to the general population, regardless of HIV status. Studies using tuberculin skin tests (TST) have reported LTBI prevalence rates among PWID ranging from 10% to 59%, and active TB prevalence rates from 5% to 66%. Evidence links TB risk primarily to injecting drug use, but smoking crack cocaine and opium also increases TB risk. In Europe, TB is the leading AIDS-defining illness among PWID. For example, in Spain, PWID are more than twice as likely to develop TB as an AIDS-defining illness compared to men who have sex with men. TB is a leading cause of death among HIV-positive PWID, with TB-associated HIV mortality rates significantly higher in this group than in the general population. There is growing evidence of an association between HIV, injecting drug use, and multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), particularly in Eastern Europe. Contributing factors to MDR-TB include incarceration and interrupted TB treatment, both of which are more common among PWID. Patients with MDR-TB, especially those with HIV-associated MDR-TB, have poor treatment outcomes and high mortality rates. Although less than 1% of the global population injects drugs, PWID account for 5–10% of all people living with HIV and nearly one-third of new HIV infections outside sub-Saharan Africa. In countries with concentrated HIV epidemics, such as those in Eastern Europe and Southeast Asia, HIV prevalence among PWID exceeds 40%. HIV transmission through shared injecting equipment and sexual transmission is also a growing concern in Africa. Additionally, PWID have the highest risk of hepatitis C infection, with a global prevalence of 67% in this group. Up to 25% of PWID with hepatitis C may also be co-infected with hepatitis B. The syndemic of TB, HIV, and viral hepatitis among PWID is a significant public health concern. Co-infection rates for hepatitis C among HIV-positive PWID approach 100% in some countries. In high TB burden countries, co-morbidity with hepatitis B and C is common among both HIV-positive and HIV-negative TB patients who inject drugs. In these settings, co-infection with TB and hepatitis C among PWID is estimated to be higher than HIV-associated TB. At least two-thirds of PWID who develop TB are estimated to have hepatitis C virus antibodies, compared to one-third who are HIV-positive. Prisons play a significant role in driving TB, HIV, and hepatitis B and C infections among PWID. The constant movement of prisoners within and outside the prison system poses challenges for continuity of care, leading to the development of MDR-TB and continued transmission within prisons and the community. TB prevalence in prisons can be 50 times higher than in the general population, and MDR-TB rates are significantly higher among prisoners. PWID experience high incarceration rates, exposing them to higher infection and TB transmission rates than the general population. Rates of HIV and hepatitis B and C infections in prisons are also considerably higher than in the community, driven by overcrowding, poor nutrition, lack of harm reduction interventions, and inadequate infection control. The purpose of these guidelines is to reduce TB and HIV-associated TB morbidity and mortality among PWID by promoting integrated delivery of comprehensive services, including TB, HIV, and viral hepatitis care, while addressing other issues such as alcohol dependence, malnutrition, mental illness, and psychosocial needs. The guidelines also address the challenges of disease control and access to services in prisons and other closed settings. The target audience for these guidelines includes policymakers, program managers, donors, development agencies, PWID networks, and advocates. The recommendations are relevant for both governmental and non-governmental sectors, including those responsible for prisons and justice systems. The guidelines emphasize the importance of human rights principles, equitable access to healthcare, and collaboration between health, social welfare, and criminal justice agencies. Access to quality healthcare is a fundamental human right, including for PWID. Healthcare providers must deliver services without discrimination, stigma, or prejudice. PWID should have access to TB, HIV, viral hepatitis, and drug dependence treatment, as well as harm reduction services, without fear of police harassment or arbitrary arrest. Services must be designed to maximize accessibility, acceptability, and quality to ensure their effectiveness. Acceptability of services is crucial for reducing the burden of TB, HIV, and viral hepatitis among PWID. Interventions must be respectful, appropriate, and affordable to ensure participation and retention in care. Collaboration between health services, PWID networks, and peer workers is essential for designing, delivering, and evaluating services. Data and medical records identifying drug users should only be used to monitor disease burden and improve service quality, not shared with law enforcement agencies.
